blocks.text: Consider a circuit consisting of a battery of emf E connected in series with a resistance R (Fig. 9.23). A steady current I flows through the circuit, and a steady potential difference V exists between the terminals A and B of the resistor. Terminal A, connected to the positive pole of the battery, is at a higher potential than terminal B. In this circuit the battery is continuously lifting charge uphill through the potential difference V. Using the meaning of potential difference, the work done in moving a charge Q up through the potential difference V is W = V x Q ... (9.38); this is the energy supplied by the battery.

The rate at which the battery supplies electrical energy is the power output, or electrical power, of the battery: electrical power = energy supplied/time taken = V Q/t. Since I = Q/t, electrical power = V x I ... (9.39). Equation 9.39 is a general relation for the power delivered from a source of current I operating at a voltage V. In the circuit of Fig. 9.23 the power supplied by the battery is expended, or dissipated, in the resistor R; by the conservation of energy, the power dissipated in the resistor is also P = V x I.

blocks.alt: A rectangular circuit: a battery E on the left side with + at the top, a resistance R on the right side between terminal A (top) and terminal B (bottom), and an arrow I along the top wire pointing right. A dotted double arrow V in the middle spans from top to bottom.
blocks.caption: Figure 9.23: The power of a battery appears as the power dissipated in the resistance R (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 9.23).

blocks.text: Alternative equations follow by substituting V = IR and I = V/R in turn: P = V x I = IR x I = I^2 R, and P = V x I = V x V/R = V^2/R. Thus there are three equations for the power dissipated in a resistor: P = V x I, P = I^2 R, P = V^2/R ... (9.40). If V is in volts and I in amperes, the power is in watts.
